sections.text: Pharmacokinetic Bioequivalence of Orforglipron Tablets and Capsules in Healthy Participants With Obesity or Overweight
ABSTRACT
Aims
To evaluate the bioequivalence of orally administered orforglipron tablets and capsules in participants with obesity or overweight who were otherwise healthy.
Materials and Methods

This phase 1, multicenter, open‐label, multiple‐dose, dose‐escalation study was conducted in 429 healthy adults. Study participants received each orforglipron capsule and tablet dose strength once daily for 7 days in the fasted state at capsule doses of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, or 36 mg and corresponding tablet doses of 0.8, 2.5, 5.5, 9, 14.5, and 17.2 mg. The primary endpoint was steady‐state area under the concentration–time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24,ss) and steady‐state maximum observed drug concentration (C max,ss). A prespecified mixed scaling approach was applied to evaluate bioequivalence. Safety and tolerability of the tablets and capsules were also assessed.
Results

Bioequivalence was demonstrated between capsules and dose‐adjusted tablets across all six doses. The 90% confidence interval of the ratios of the geometric least‐squares means of AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss between each capsule dose and corresponding tablet dose met the predefined criteria for bioequivalence. The safety profiles were similar between tablets and capsules, with no apparent differences or trends in the incidence of treatment‐emergent adverse events by presentation or with increasing dose.
Conclusions

Once‐daily orforglipron capsules and dose‐adjusted tablets demonstrated pharmacokinetic bioequivalence at all tested doses and showed similar safety and tolerability profiles, with mostly mild treatment‐emergent adverse events consistent with previous orforglipron clinical trials.
ClinicalTrials .gov Identifier: NCT06440980.
Introduction

Currently approved glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonists (GLP‐1 RAs) are peptide‐based agents that require subcutaneous injection or oral administration and are associated with restrictions on food and water intake. There is an unmet need for effective, safe, and well‐tolerated oral formulations of GLP‐1 RAs for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight that can be administered without food‐ or water‐related dosing restrictions.

Orforglipron is an oral, once‐daily, non‐peptide, small‐molecule GLP‐1 RA that has been developed as both capsules and tablets and can be administered with no restrictions on food and water intake. In the ATTAIN‐1, ATTAIN‐2, and ACHIEVE‐3 phase 3 trials, once‐daily treatment with orally administered orforglipron capsules was associated with superior weight reduction and glycemic control compared with placebo and superior glycemic control compared with oral semaglutide, with a safety profile similar to that of approved GLP‐1 RAs. Orforglipron capsules at doses of 6, 12, and 36 mg were studied in these trials, with dose escalation through 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 mg. The orforglipron tablets were later developed to allow increased flexibility of treatment options. Establishing bioequivalence between orforglipron tablets and capsules is important to ensure equivalent therapeutic effects and safety across dosage forms. Here, we report results from a phase 1 pharmacokinetics (PK) study that assessed the bioequivalence of orforglipron tablets and capsules at all dose strengths among participants with obesity or overweight who were otherwise healthy.
Methods
Study Design

This was a phase 1, multicenter, open‐label, randomized, multiple‐dose, dose‐escalation study of orforglipron tablets and capsules in participants with obesity or overweight (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06440980). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the studies were conducted in accordance with the principles derived from international guidelines including the Declaration of Helsinki and Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences International Ethical Guidelines, the principles of Good Clinical Practice as defined by the International Conference on Harmonization, and all applicable laws and regulations. The study was designed in consideration of guidance provided by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the International Conference on Harmonization on the design and conduct of bioequivalence studies.

Based on the steady‐state area under the concentration–time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24,ss) and steady‐state maximum observed drug concentration (C max,ss) observed in a pilot study of relative bioavailability for both capsules and tablets, the corresponding tablet dose strengths of 0.8, 2.5, 5.5, 9, 14.5, and 17.2 mg were selected to be evaluated with capsule dose strengths of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 mg. Given the difference in drug absorption between the two drug products, the tablet dose strengths are numerically lower than the capsule dose strengths, particularly at higher doses. Therefore, the bioequivalence between capsules and corresponding tablets was assessed on a dose‐adjusted basis.

Study participants received once‐daily doses of orally administered orforglipron tablets or capsules in a partial replicated crossover manner according to the dose‐escalation schedule shown in Figure 1.
Schematic overview of the study. CRU, clinical research unit.

The study included two cohorts. Participants in Cohort 1 received inpatient treatment at a clinical research unit (CRU) for the full nine periods of study dosing (9 weeks), while participants in Cohort 2 self‐administered treatment at home (after receiving training on in‐home dosing) for periods 1 to 6 during initial dose escalation (6 weeks) and then received inpatient treatment at the CRU for periods 7 through 15 of dosing (9 weeks) (Figure 1). Each dosing period of the study lasted 7 days. Participants in both cohorts were randomly assigned 1:1:1 to one of three dosing sequences. Participants in Cohort 1 initially received orforglipron at the 1‐mg capsule or 0.8‐mg tablet dose, then had their dose escalated in a crossover manner to the 3‐mg and 6‐mg capsules and the corresponding 2.5‐mg and 5.5‐mg tablets over a 9‐week period. Participants in Cohort 2 self‐administered doses of orforglipron at home starting with the 1‐mg capsule and escalating to the 3‐mg and 6‐mg capsules over 6 weeks; after that time, participants in Cohort 2 received inpatient dosing at the CRU starting with the 12‐mg capsule or 9‐mg tablet and had their dose escalated in a crossover manner to the 24‐mg and 36‐mg capsules and the corresponding 14.5‐mg and 17.2‐mg tablets over 9 weeks. Both cohorts included a third week at each capsule dose strength for each crossover to allow for assessment of within‐participant PK variability for capsules. In this three‐way partial replicate design, each participant received the reference treatment (capsule) in two separate periods and the test treatment (tablet) in one period for each capsule dose level. This allowed for use of a reference‐scaled approach to assess bioequivalence at the capsule dose strengths if the within‐participant standard deviation (S wr) was ≥ 0.294 (see Section 2.4).

Consistent with FDA guidance for bioequivalence studies, during inpatient dosing at the CRU, participants received orforglipron tablets or capsules each morning while in a seated position, following an overnight fast of ≥ 10 h, with ~240 mL of water at room temperature. Participants who self‐administered orforglipron capsules at home were also advised to take 1 capsule with ~240 mL of water at room temperature after an overnight fast of ≥ 10 h.
Participants

The study included adults aged 18 to 65 years with a body mass index of ≥ 27 to ≤ 40 kg/m2. Participants were overtly healthy based on their medical history and a physical examination and had a ≤ 5% gain or loss in body weight for 1 month before screening. Participants were excluded if they had glycated haemoglobin ≥ 6.5%, were exposed to GLP‐1 analogs or related compounds within 3 months of screening, or had taken any remedies intended to promote weight loss within 14 days before screening.
The safety population consisted of all participants exposed to ≥ 1 dose of orforglipron. The PK population comprised all participants in the safety population who had evaluable PK data.
Endpoints and Assessments

The primary endpoint was assessment of AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss for evaluation of the bioequivalence between orforglipron tablets and capsules at capsule doses of 3, 6, 12, and 36 mg. Secondary endpoints were assessment of AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss for bioequivalence evaluation of orforglipron tablets and capsules at capsule doses of 1 and 24 mg, which serve as intermediate titration doses to mitigate gastrointestinal adverse events during dose escalation, as well as assessment of safety and tolerability of tablets and capsules, including serious adverse events (AEs) and treatment‐emergent AEs (TEAEs).
Bioanalysis of Orforglipron in Plasma

Orforglipron in human plasma with K2EDTA anticoagulant was measured by Q 2 Solutions (Ithaca, New York, USA). In plasma, orforglipron was extracted by protein precipitation with separation by high‐performance liquid chromatography. Detection was provided by a SCIEX API 6500 mass spectrometer using turbo ion spray in the positive ionization mode. The internal standard was a stable isotope‐labelled orforglipron, orforglipron‐d6 (Chugai Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). The validated assay range was 0.100 to 100.000 ng/mL. During validation, inter‐batch precision and accuracy were ≤ 9%.

Study samples above the limit of quantitation were diluted and reanalyzed to yield results within the calibrated range. For quantitation of orforglipron in study plasma samples, the percentage relative error was < 1% and percentage relative standard deviation of quality control samples was < 15%.
Pharmacokinetic Analysis

Plasma PK parameters were calculated using steady‐state PK data from periods 1 to 15 (where available) following 7 days of repeated once‐daily oral dosing. On day 7 of each treatment period, blood samples of ~2 mL each were collected for PK assessments before dosing and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, and 24 h after dosing. Comparisons were performed separately for each of the six capsules and corresponding tablets. PK parameter estimates were determined using noncompartmental methods with Phoenix WinNonlin version 8.3.5. Data were excluded from the primary statistical analysis if the participant had an AE of vomiting that occurred at or before two times the median time of maximum observed drug concentration (t max) for the dosing regimen, if the participant did not take the capsule or tablet at the start of the steady‐state PK assessment period (day 7), or if they missed a dose on days 4 to 6 in a given treatment week but took the dose at the start of day 7. Arithmetic mean concentration–time profiles were plotted using nominal PK sampling time points per the protocol. Mean concentrations were plotted for a given time if two‐thirds of the individual data at that time point had quantifiable measurements within the sampling window (±10%).
For the safety and tolerability assessment, the frequency and number of TEAEs, including treatment‐related TEAEs, were summarized.
Statistical Analysis

A prespecified mixed scaling approach was used to establish bioequivalence. Two one‐sided t‐tests were applied to the geometric mean ratio (GMR) between the AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss of each dose using the capsule as the reference and the corresponding tablet as the test.

The S wr of the reference capsule at each dose level was estimated based on the difference in the log‐transformed PK parameter calculated between the two capsule dosing periods from each participant at each dose level. At doses with an estimated S wr ≥ 0.294, the reference‐scaled procedure was applied to determine bioequivalence for each parameter of interest. A linear model for each parameter was fit using the sequence as a fixed effect and the difference between the test and reference on a log scale as the response variable. Bioequivalence was concluded if the point estimate of the estimated test and reference GMR was within 0.8 to 1.25 and the 90% confidence interval (CI) of the GMR was within 0.8Swr/0.25 to 1.25Swr/0.25. At doses with an estimated S wr < 0.294, two one‐sided t‐tests were used to determine bioequivalence for individual PK parameters with a bioequivalent boundary of 0.8 to 1.25. The natural log‐transformed AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss were analysed using a linear mixed model at each capsule dose level with the corresponding tablet dose. The model included treatment sequence, treatment period (1 week each), and treatment (capsule and corresponding tablet) as fixed effects and participant as a random effect while allowing for different within‐participant variability for each dosage form.

The t max was analysed nonparametrically. Estimates of the median of within‐participant differences and approximate 90% CIs were calculated using the Hahn–Meeker method along with p values based on the Wilcoxon signed‐rank test.

Unscaled analyses were performed for all capsule doses: as the primary method for doses with S wr < 0.294, and additionally as a secondary/sensitivity analysis for doses with S wr ≥ 0.294, where reference‐scaled methods were used as the primary analysis. A sample size of ~400 participants was planned so that ~150 participants with evaluable PK data in each cohort would complete the study. This sample size was selected to provide a ≥ 90% chance to ensure that the 90% CI of the GMR of AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss between the tablet (test) and capsule (reference) of a given dose level would fall within the equivalence boundary using a mixed scaling approach, assuming an expected GMR of 1.09 (test vs. reference) and a within‐participant coefficient of variation of 40%.
Results
Participants

The participant flow throughout the study is shown in Figure S1. A total of 429 participants received ≥ 1 dose of orforglipron (safety population), and 398 had evaluable PK data (PK population). Overall, 373 participants completed the study and 56 discontinued. Baseline characteristics were similar across the two cohorts (Table 1). There were 254 (59.2%) male and 175 (40.8%) female participants that ranged in age from 19 to 65 years and in body mass index from 26.9 to 39.9 kg/m2. The duration of treatment among participants ranged from 9 to 18 weeks.

Pharmacokinetics

The arithmetic mean plasma concentration–time profile of orforglipron on day 7 for all doses is presented in Figure 2. Following once‐daily oral dosing of orforglipron tablets and capsules, C max,ss was reached at a median of ~4 to 8 h on the day of PK assessment, which was comparable between tablets and capsules. After C max,ss was reached, plasma concentrations appeared to decline in a biphasic manner.

Arithmetic mean (standard deviation) plasma concentration–time profiles of orforglipron on day 7 after tablet or capsule administration in the pharmacokinetics population. Doses listed are the reference capsule doses. The black dashed line represents the lower limit of quantification (0.100 ng/mL).

The 90% CI of the ratios of geometric least‐squares means for the corresponding doses of tablets versus capsules for AUC0–24,ss and C max,ss demonstrated bioequivalence between tablets and capsules at each of the six doses for both primary and secondary PK endpoints (Table S1; Figure 3). For primary and secondary endpoint analyses that utilized an unscaled approach for capsule doses with an S wr ≥ 0.294, results were similar to those of the reference‐scaled approach, and bioequivalence was observed again at all capsule doses (Table S2).

Safety

Safety profiles were similar between capsules and tablets, and there were no apparent differences or trends in the incidence of TEAEs between formulations or with increasing dose. A total of 89% of participants reported ≥ 1 TEAE (Table S3). The most common TEAEs were constipation (54%), nausea (44%), and headache (42%). Of all TEAEs, 98% (n = 2497/2543) were reported as mild. Three participants (0.7%) experienced serious AEs (oesophageal carcinoma considered by the investigator to be not related to study treatment, cholecystitis acute considered related to study treatment by the investigator, and atrial fibrillation considered related to study treatment by the investigator), and 15 (4%) discontinued due to AEs. No deaths were reported during the study. Consistent with the known secondary pharmacological effects of GLP‐1 RAs, a general decrease from baseline in mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure and a general increase in mean pulse rate were observed throughout the study (data not shown). Eight participants were reported with TEAEs related to elevated alanine or aspartate aminotransferase levels. Three of the eight participants experienced TEAEs related to elevated levels of both aspartate and alanine aminotransferases; one discontinued treatment as a result, and the elevations were resolved. There were no other clinically meaningful changes in laboratory values observed during the study.
Discussion

This PK study demonstrated bioequivalence between all doses of orforglipron capsules and corresponding tablets in participants with obesity or overweight who were otherwise healthy. All previously generated phase 3 clinical data for orforglipron from participants with obesity or overweight and those with type 2 diabetes have been for a capsule presentation. The current study demonstrates bioequivalence between dose strengths of orforglipron capsules and corresponding tablets for each of the six doses tested. Additionally, the safety profiles of all doses were similar when administered as tablets or capsules and were consistent with the known safety profile of the GLP‐1 RA class.

The design of the study was informed and optimized based on the PK and pharmacodynamic properties of orforglipron from previous clinical pharmacology studies. Given the pharmacological activity of orforglipron and the duration needed to escalate to the highest dose strength, participants were expected to lose weight during the study. Participants with obesity or overweight who were otherwise healthy were enrolled to adequately balance the benefits and risks to participants in this phase 1 study.

Gastrointestinal AEs, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and constipation, are known to be associated with GLP‐1 pharmacology. Vomiting can impact PK data due to the loss of administered study drug in the vomitus. These effects can be minimized through dose escalation. Therefore, to allow assessment of bioequivalence at multiple dose strengths, a dose‐escalation study with repeat dosing at each dose level was necessary, followed by assessment of PK at steady state.

A partial replicated design was adopted in this study based on a previous unpublished study (NCT05841238) in which the intra‐participant variability for orforglipron capsules was evaluated (coefficient of variation > 30% for AUC and > 40% for C max). This design enabled accurate determination of intra‐participant variability in the bioequivalence analysis with use of a mixed scaling approach, aligning with FDA guidelines for determining bioequivalence.

Only healthy individuals with obesity or overweight were included, and most participants were male. However, an unpublished covariate analysis conducted during Phase 3 studies demonstrated that sex and diabetes disease status do not have a clinically meaningful impact on orforglipron PK, and other intrinsic factors that may potentially affect PK were accounted for through the crossover design of the study reported here. Therefore, the demonstration of bioequivalence between capsules and tablets applies across all populations and indications for which orforglipron capsules have been studied.
Conclusion

Findings from this study establish the bioequivalence between all orforglipron capsule doses and corresponding tablet doses studied, with no new safety concerns identified. Given the confirmation of bioequivalence in this study, it is expected that the safety and efficacy of the orforglipron capsule doses studied in the phase 3 studies will be equivalent to that of the corresponding orforglipron tablet doses.

Supporting information
Data Availability Statement

Lilly provides access to all individual participant data collected during the trial, after anonymization, with the exception of pharmacokinetic or genetic data. Data are available to request 6 months after the indication studied has been approved in the US and EU and after primary publication acceptance, whichever is later. No expiration date of data requests is currently set once data are made available. Access is provided after a proposal has been approved by an independent review committee identified for this purpose and after receipt of a signed data sharing agreement. Data and documents, including the study protocol, statistical analysis plan, clinical study report, blank or annotated case report forms, will be provided in a secure data sharing environment. For details on submitting a request, see the instructions provided at www.vivli.org.
